short: Tax and welfare rules that cushion the economy on their own: governments collect less tax and pay out more support when times turn bad.
kid: When a friend has a slow day at the lemonade stand, the group lets them keep more and gives them a little extra help. On a great day, they share a bit more back. Nobody has to decide each time; it just happens.
detail: Automatic stabilisers are features of the budget that push against the business cycle without any new decision by the government. In a downturn, incomes and profits fall, so tax collections fall, with progressive income tax and corporate tax dropping faster than the economy, while spending on unemployment benefits and welfare rises. The deficit widens and props up household spending. In a boom the opposite happens, cooling demand. They act faster than discretionary policy, which needs debate and legislation. Their strength depends on how large and progressive the tax-and-transfer system is: they are big in Europe, with generous jobless benefits, and smaller in India, where many workers are informal and few pay income tax. For investors, they explain why deficits swell in recessions even without stimulus. Common confusion: a deficit that widens this way is cyclical, not a deliberate loosening of policy.
example: Say a country's tax take is 20% of a $1,000 billion economy, or $200 billion. In a recession the economy shrinks 5% to $950 billion and, because of progressive rates, the tax take falls to 19% of it, or $180.5 billion. Jobless benefits also rise by $15 billion, so the deficit widens by $19.5 billion + $15 billion = $34.5 billion with no new law passed.

short: How much a country's total output changes for each rupee or dollar of extra government spending or tax cuts.
kid: You pay a friend to help paint your fence. Your friend uses that money to buy lemonade, and the lemonade seller buys crayons. One payment keeps moving and helps lots of people.
detail: The fiscal multiplier is the change in GDP caused by a change in government spending or taxes, divided by the size of that change. A multiplier of 1.5 means ₹100 of spending lifts output by ₹150, because the contractor's workers spend their wages, shopkeepers spend their takings, and so on. Leakages shrink the effect: saving, taxes, imports, and crowding out if heavy borrowing pushes up interest rates. Multipliers tend to be larger in recessions, when workers and machines sit idle and central banks hold rates low, and smaller when the economy is near full capacity. Studies for India, including by NIPFP and the RBI, find multipliers for capital expenditure well above those for revenue spending such as salaries and subsidies, which underpins the push on public capex. Common confusion: the textbook formula 1/(1-MPC) overstates real-world multipliers, which are estimated from data.
example: Say a government spends an extra ₹1 lakh crore on roads and, over two years, GDP ends up ₹2.5 lakh crore higher than it otherwise would have been. The multiplier is 2.5. In the simple textbook model, if households spend 60% of every extra rupee (MPC = 0.6), the multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 2.5.
formula: Fiscal multiplier = Change in GDP / Change in government spending (or taxes); simple Keynesian multiplier = 1 / (1 - MPC)

short: Government spending that creates lasting assets such as roads, railways and ports, plus loans to states and investments in public sector companies.
kid: Spending your pocket money on sweets is fun, but they are gone by tomorrow. Buying a bicycle is different, because you can ride it for years. When the town builds a road or a bridge, that is like buying the bicycle.
detail: In India's budget, capital expenditure covers capital outlay on assets such as highways, railways, defence equipment and buildings, plus loans and advances to states and public sector companies. It either creates an asset or reduces a liability, unlike revenue expenditure. Since 2020 the Centre has made capex a main growth lever, including 50-year interest-free loans to states for their own projects. Effective capital expenditure adds grants given to states and others for creating capital assets, which sit in revenue expenditure in the Centre's books but still build assets. Markets track it because it drives orders for cement, steel, capital goods and construction companies, and because capex is thought to have a larger growth multiplier than subsidies. Common confusion: budgeted capex is a target, and actual spending often falls short when ministries or states spend slowly, so check the monthly accounts and revised estimates.
example: Say the Centre budgets ₹11 lakh crore of capital expenditure and ₹4 lakh crore of grants to states for building assets. Effective capital expenditure is ₹15 lakh crore. If only ₹7.7 lakh crore of the capex has been spent by the end of December, that is 70% of the target with a quarter of the year left.
formula: Effective capital expenditure = Capital expenditure + Grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets

short: Government spending on running costs, such as salaries, pensions, interest and subsidies, that creates no lasting asset.
kid: Some money is spent on things that are used up the same day, like lunch and bus rides. The town does this too when it pays its teachers and keeps the street lights on.
detail: Revenue expenditure is government spending that neither creates an asset nor reduces a liability. It covers salaries, pensions, interest on debt, subsidies, the running costs of ministries and most grants to states. For India's Centre, interest payments are the single largest item, taking roughly a quarter of total spending in recent budgets. Grants to states count here even when states use them to build assets, which is why the budget also reports effective capital expenditure. When revenue expenditure exceeds revenue receipts, the gap is the revenue deficit: the government is borrowing to pay running costs, like borrowing to pay the grocery bill. Investors watch the mix, because a high share of committed items such as interest, salaries and pensions leaves less room for capex. Common confusion: 'revenue' here means recurring, not income; revenue expenditure is spending, not earnings.
example: Say a government's revenue expenditure is ₹39 lakh crore and its revenue receipts are ₹34 lakh crore. The revenue deficit is ₹5 lakh crore, money borrowed to pay running costs. If interest payments alone are ₹12.5 lakh crore, they use up about 37% of revenue receipts.
formula: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure - Revenue receipts

short: Government income it never has to repay and that does not come from selling assets: mainly taxes, plus fees, interest and dividends.
kid: Pocket money from grandma and coins earned by doing chores are yours to keep. You never have to give them back, and you did not sell any toys to get them.
detail: Revenue receipts are receipts that neither create a liability nor reduce the government's assets. They have two parts. Tax revenue is income tax, corporation tax, GST, customs and excise; for the Centre it is counted net of the states' share, since devolved taxes belong to the states. Non-tax revenue is dividends from the RBI and public sector companies, interest on loans, fees, and spectrum and other licence payments. Revenue receipts are meant to pay for revenue expenditure, and the gap between the two is the revenue deficit. Their growth depends on nominal GDP growth and tax buoyancy, so a slowdown in nominal growth shows up here quickly. Common confusion: disinvestment proceeds and loan recoveries are not revenue receipts, even though they bring in cash without borrowing; they are non-debt capital receipts, because the government gives up an asset to get them.
example: Say the Centre's net tax revenue is ₹28 lakh crore and its non-tax revenue, including the RBI's surplus transfer, is ₹5.8 lakh crore. Revenue receipts are ₹33.8 lakh crore. If revenue expenditure is ₹39 lakh crore, the revenue deficit is ₹5.2 lakh crore.
formula: Revenue receipts = Net tax revenue + Non-tax revenue

short: Government receipts that either create a debt, such as borrowing, or reduce its assets, such as selling stakes in public companies or recovering loans.
kid: You can get money for a new bike in two ways: borrow from your big sister and pay her back later, or sell some old toys. Both give you money now, but either you owe something or you have fewer toys.
detail: Capital receipts are receipts that create a liability or run down the government's assets. Most are borrowings: market loans through dated securities and treasury bills, securities issued against small savings, and other liabilities. The rest are non-debt capital receipts, or NDCR: recoveries of loans given earlier, disinvestment proceeds from selling shares in public sector companies, and other miscellaneous receipts. NDCR matter because they reduce the fiscal deficit, which is total spending minus revenue receipts and NDCR; borrowing fills the remaining gap. For bond markets, a shortfall in disinvestment usually means more borrowing or spending cuts elsewhere. Common confusion: capital receipts are not income. Borrowing must be repaid with interest, and a stake can be sold only once, so a budget that leans on one-off asset sales is weaker than it looks.
example: Say a government spends ₹50 lakh crore, collects ₹34 lakh crore in revenue receipts, and plans ₹0.5 lakh crore of disinvestment and ₹0.3 lakh crore of loan recoveries. Non-debt capital receipts are ₹0.8 lakh crore, so the fiscal deficit is ₹50 - ₹34 - ₹0.8 = ₹15.2 lakh crore, which is borrowed. Total capital receipts are ₹0.8 + ₹15.2 = ₹16 lakh crore.
formula: Capital receipts = Borrowings and other liabilities + Non-debt capital receipts; Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure - (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts)

short: Payments or price support from the government that make goods like food, fertiliser or fuel cheaper for buyers than their actual cost.
kid: The school sells lunch for less than it costs to make, and the town pays the rest so every child can eat. The town's helping hand makes lunch cheaper for everyone.
detail: A subsidy is government support that lowers the price a buyer pays or raises what a producer receives. India's three big central subsidies are food, mainly free grain distributed through the FCI and ration shops under the rules as of 2025; fertiliser, chiefly urea sold at a fixed low price with makers paid the difference; and petroleum, now mostly LPG support for poorer households. Subsidies can also be hidden, as tax breaks, cheap credit or regulated prices that state firms absorb. The bill swings with global prices: when gas and fertiliser prices spiked after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, India's fertiliser subsidy more than doubled from its pre-pandemic level. For markets, overruns threaten deficit targets, and delayed payments squeeze fertiliser and oil marketing companies. Common confusion: a subsidy is not always a cash payment; forcing a seller to sell below cost is one too.
example: Say urea costs a fertiliser company ₹2,400 per 45 kg bag to make and deliver, but the farmer pays a fixed, government-set ₹250. The government pays the company the gap of ₹2,150 per bag, so 40 crore bags cost it ₹86,000 crore in a year.
formula: Subsidy per unit = Cost of supply - Price charged to the buyer

short: Borrowing done by government-owned bodies on the government's behalf and repaid from its budget, but kept out of the official deficit figures.
kid: Your mum says you can only borrow two toys this week. So you ask your little brother to borrow a third toy for you. Your count says two, but really you have three.
detail: Off-budget borrowing, also called extra-budgetary resources, is debt raised by public sector companies, agencies or special-purpose vehicles to fund government spending, with interest and repayment met from the budget. Because the borrower is not the government itself, the debt does not show up in the fiscal deficit, which flatters it. In India, the FCI for years borrowed from the National Small Savings Fund to cover unpaid food subsidy bills, until the 2021-22 budget moved that spending back on to the books. States have used their own corporations in the same way; since 2022 the Centre counts such borrowing, when serviced from a state's budget, against that state's borrowing limit. Bond investors and rating agencies treat the true deficit as the reported deficit plus these liabilities. Common confusion: not all borrowing by public companies is off-budget; it counts only when the budget, not the company's own revenue, repays it.
example: Say a government reports a fiscal deficit of ₹13.5 lakh crore, 4.5% of a ₹300 lakh crore GDP. If state-owned bodies have also borrowed ₹1.5 lakh crore that the budget will repay, the true deficit is ₹15 lakh crore, or 5% of GDP.
formula: Adjusted fiscal deficit = Reported fiscal deficit + Off-budget borrowing serviced from the budget

short: The surplus profit the Reserve Bank of India transfers to the central government each year after setting aside money for its own reserves.
kid: The big family piggy bank earns a little extra over the year. Grandpa keeps some aside for rainy days and gives the rest to the family to use.
detail: The RBI is wholly owned by the government, and Section 47 of the RBI Act requires it to pass on its surplus profit after making provisions. Its income comes mainly from interest on government bonds and foreign assets and from gains when it sells foreign currency; its costs include printing notes and interest paid when it absorbs surplus liquidity. How much it retains is governed by the Economic Capital Framework adopted in 2019, which sets a range for its contingent risk buffer as a share of the balance sheet; under the rules as of 2025, it is 4.5-7.5%. The transfer is now a large non-tax revenue item: ₹2.69 lakh crore for 2024-25, paid in May 2025, a record at the time. A bigger-than-budgeted payout can cut government borrowing and ease bond yields. Common confusion: it is not a dividend on listed shares but a surplus transfer to the sole owner.
example: Say the RBI earns ₹3.5 lakh crore in a year, spends ₹0.4 lakh crore on running costs and sets aside ₹0.6 lakh crore to keep its risk buffer in the target range. It transfers the remaining ₹2.5 lakh crore. If the government had budgeted ₹2 lakh crore, the extra ₹0.5 lakh crore can lower its borrowing or cover spending overruns.
formula: Surplus transferred = RBI income - RBI expenditure - Provisions (including the contingent risk buffer)

short: How strongly a government's tax collections respond to growth in the economy: the percentage rise in tax revenue for each 1% rise in GDP.
kid: When the whole town earns more, it also puts more into the shared jar for parks and schools. Sometimes the jar fills up even faster than the town's earnings grow.
detail: Tax buoyancy is the ratio of the growth rate of tax revenue to the growth rate of nominal GDP. A buoyancy above 1 means taxes are growing faster than the economy, so the tax-to-GDP ratio rises; below 1, it falls. It includes the effect of changes in tax rates, bases and enforcement, which sets it apart from tax elasticity, which strips out discretionary policy changes to show the tax system's built-in response. In India, assumed buoyancy drives budget revenue targets: a buoyancy of 1.1 on 10% nominal growth implies tax growth of 11%. Formalisation, GST and better compliance have lifted buoyancy in some years, while rate cuts lower it. Common confusion: buoyancy uses nominal GDP, not real GDP, so a fall in inflation can hurt tax growth even when the real economy is doing fine. Single-year figures are noisy, so look at multi-year averages.
example: Say gross tax revenue rises from ₹35 lakh crore to ₹39.2 lakh crore, a 12% increase, while nominal GDP grows 10%. Tax buoyancy is 12 / 10 = 1.2, so the tax-to-GDP ratio rises.
formula: Tax buoyancy = % change in tax revenue / % change in nominal GDP

short: Total tax collected in a year as a share of the economy's size, showing how much of national income the government takes in tax.
kid: We look at all the food the whole town makes in a year. Then we see how much of it goes into the shared basket for parks and schools.
detail: The tax-to-GDP ratio divides total tax revenue by nominal GDP for the same year. It measures a government's capacity to fund spending without borrowing, and is compared across countries and over time. Rich OECD economies collect around a third of GDP in tax on average, while many emerging markets collect less than a fifth. India's combined Centre and state ratio has been around 17-18% of GDP in recent years, and the Centre's gross tax revenue about 11-12%, held back by a large informal sector and a narrow income-tax base. Rating agencies watch it because a low ratio leaves less room to service debt. Always check whether a figure covers only the central government or all levels, and whether social security contributions are included, as OECD figures do. Common confusion: a rising ratio can come from better compliance and formalisation, not just higher tax rates.
example: Say a country collects ₹54 lakh crore in taxes across all levels of government in a year when nominal GDP is ₹300 lakh crore. Its tax-to-GDP ratio is 54 / 300 = 18%.
formula: Tax-to-GDP ratio = Total tax revenue / Nominal GDP x 100

short: An idea showing that tax revenue rises with tax rates only up to a point, after which higher rates can bring in less money.
kid: If you ask friends to bring one sweet each for the party jar, the jar fills up. If you ask for all their sweets, they might stop bringing any, and the jar stays empty.
detail: The Laffer curve, popularised by economist Arthur Laffer in the 1970s, plots tax revenue against the tax rate. At a 0% rate the government collects nothing, and at 100% it also collects almost nothing, because nobody has a reason to earn, report or keep income there. Somewhere in between is a revenue-maximising rate. Above it, cutting rates can raise revenue by encouraging work, investment and honest reporting. The idea was used to argue for the US tax cuts of the 1980s. The hard part is knowing where the peak lies: most studies place it well above the rates most large economies charge on ordinary incomes, so broad tax cuts usually lose revenue, even if they help growth. Common confusion: the curve does not say tax cuts always pay for themselves; that holds only if rates start above the peak.
example: Say at a 30% rate people report ₹100 crore of taxable income, raising ₹30 crore. If the rate goes to 40% and reported income falls to ₹70 crore through less work and more avoidance, revenue drops to ₹28 crore. In this case the higher rate is past the peak.
formula: Tax revenue = Tax rate x Tax base, where the tax base shrinks as the rate rises

short: When unchanged tax thresholds quietly raise the tax burden as incomes rise with inflation, or more broadly when tight budgets slow economic growth.
kid: Your shoes stay the same size while your feet keep growing, so they pinch a little more each month. Nobody changed the shoes, but they feel tighter.
detail: Fiscal drag has two related meanings. The narrow one: if income tax slabs, allowances and thresholds are not raised with inflation, rising pay pushes people into higher brackets, so they hand over a larger share of income in tax even though their real income has not grown. This is bracket creep, a silent tax rise that needs no new law; the UK's freeze of income tax thresholds from 2021 is a well-known example. The broader meaning: any fiscal tightening, such as higher taxes or spending cuts, that subtracts from GDP growth, as when stimulus programmes expire. In both senses it is a headwind for consumer spending. In India, slabs are revised only occasionally in budgets, so inflation erodes them between revisions. Common confusion: fiscal drag is not a rise in tax rates; the burden grows through inflation and frozen thresholds alone.
example: Say income up to $50,000 is taxed at 10% and anything above at 30%. A worker earning $48,000 pays $4,800. If inflation is 5% and her pay rises to $50,400 while the threshold stays put, she pays $5,000 + $120 = $5,120, about 6.7% more tax on a pay rise that only keeps up with prices.

short: How taxing and spending powers, and the money itself, are divided between a country's central government and its states or regions.
kid: Mum collects all the pocket money in one jar, but each child looks after their own room and garden. So she shares the jar fairly, giving a bit more to the child with the biggest garden.
detail: Fiscal federalism is about how a federal country splits responsibilities and revenues across levels of government. In India the Seventh Schedule gives the Centre the most buoyant taxes, such as income and corporation tax, while states carry much of the spending on health, police, agriculture and education. This vertical imbalance is closed by transfers: tax devolution recommended by the Finance Commission, which sets the states' share of the divisible pool (41% for 2021-26 under the 15th Commission; the 16th covers 2026-31) and how it is split among states, plus grants and centrally sponsored schemes. Since 2017, GST has pooled most indirect taxes, with rates set in the GST Council. For bond investors, state borrowing through SDLs and disputes over cesses kept outside the divisible pool both flow from this design. Common confusion: vertical devolution is the Centre-states split; horizontal devolution is how the states' share is divided among them.
example: Say the divisible pool is ₹36 lakh crore and the states' share is 41%. Vertical devolution gives the states ₹14.76 lakh crore together. If one state's horizontal share is 10%, it receives ₹1.476 lakh crore, about ₹1.48 lakh crore.

short: When a government's heavy borrowing needs force the central bank to keep interest rates low or fund deficits, even if inflation rises.
kid: A babysitter is meant to decide bedtime, but the big brother keeps begging to stay up, and the babysitter always gives in. Soon, bedtime means nothing.
detail: Under fiscal dominance, monetary policy is set to keep government debt affordable rather than to control inflation. It can be explicit, when the central bank buys government bonds directly or caps yields to fund deficits, or implicit, when it holds back from raising rates because higher rates would swell the interest bill on a large debt. The danger is that markets stop believing the inflation target, expectations rise and the currency weakens. India had a form of it until the 1990s, when the RBI automatically financed deficits through ad hoc treasury bills; that ended in 1997, and the FRBM Act later barred the RBI from buying government bonds at primary auctions except in special circumstances. Political pressure on the US Federal Reserve in 2025 revived the debate. Common confusion: crisis-time bond buying to hit an inflation target, such as quantitative easing, is not by itself fiscal dominance.
example: Say a government owes $30 trillion and its economy produces $25 trillion a year. If the average interest rate on that debt eventually rises by 2 percentage points, the yearly interest bill grows by $600 billion, or 2.4% of GDP. Fear of that cost is what tempts governments to lean on the central bank.

short: The theory that people save a government's debt-funded tax cut, expecting higher taxes later to repay the debt, so their spending does not change.
kid: If grandma gives you ten sweets today but says she will need ten sweets back next week, you would not eat them. You would keep them safe so you can give them back.
detail: Ricardian equivalence, named after David Ricardo and formalised by Robert Barro in 1974, says that for a given path of government spending it makes no difference whether the government pays with taxes now or with borrowing now. Borrowing today means higher taxes tomorrow, and forward-looking households see that, so they save the whole tax cut to meet the future bill. Consumption, and therefore demand, stays the same, and a deficit-financed stimulus does nothing. The result needs strong assumptions: people are rational and far-sighted, care about their heirs, can borrow and save freely, and taxes do not distort behaviour. In practice many households spend part of a tax cut, especially those short of cash, so the full result rarely holds, but it helps explain why stimulus can be weaker when the public worries about debt. Common confusion: Ricardo himself doubted it held in practice.
example: Say the government cuts each household's tax by $1,000 this year and borrows the money at 5%, planning to raise taxes by $1,050 next year to repay it. A Ricardian household saves the $1,000 at 5%, has exactly $1,050 next year to pay the higher tax, and spends nothing extra in between.

short: A US law capping the total debt the federal government may owe; Congress must raise or suspend it before borrowing can go past it.
kid: Your parents say you can only owe your sister five sweets at a time. To borrow a sixth, they must agree to a new rule first, even to pay for sweets you already ate.
detail: The debt ceiling, or debt limit, caps the total amount of debt the US Treasury can have outstanding. It does not authorise new spending; it limits borrowing to pay for spending and tax cuts Congress has already approved. When debt hits the limit, Treasury uses accounting steps called extraordinary measures, plus its cash balance, to keep paying bills. The X-date is when those run out and the government could miss payments, including on Treasuries. Standoffs have rattled markets: in 2011, S&P cut the US rating from AAA to AA+. Bills maturing near the X-date sell off, and once the limit is lifted Treasury sells a wave of bills to rebuild its cash, draining liquidity. The limit was suspended in 2023 and raised by $5 trillion in July 2025. Common confusion: a debt-ceiling fight is not a government shutdown, which happens when spending bills are not passed.
example: When the debt limit was reinstated in January 2025, it stood at about $36.1 trillion. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act raised it by $5 trillion in July 2025, to about $41.1 trillion. In the months between, the Treasury relied on extraordinary measures and its cash balance to pay bills.

short: A halt to non-essential US federal government work when Congress fails to pass the funding laws that let agencies spend money.
kid: If the grown-ups can't agree on the shopping list, nobody goes to the shop. The house keeps the most important things running, but snacks and outings stop until they agree.
detail: In the US, agencies can spend only what Congress appropriates through annual spending bills or a stopgap continuing resolution. If none is in place when the fiscal year starts on 1 October, or a stopgap expires, the Antideficiency Act forces unfunded agencies to stop non-essential work. Hundreds of thousands of federal workers are furloughed or work without pay, and have usually been paid later; essential services, Social Security payments and interest on Treasuries continue. Markets tend to shrug off short shutdowns, but long ones dent GDP, delay data such as the monthly jobs and inflation reports, and cloud the Federal Reserve's view of the economy. The 43-day shutdown of October-November 2025 was the longest on record at the time. Common confusion: a shutdown is not a debt default; it concerns permission to spend, while the debt ceiling concerns permission to borrow.
example: The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the 35-day shutdown of December 2018 to January 2019 reduced US GDP by $11 billion, of which about $3 billion was never recovered. The other $8 billion was made up later as delayed spending resumed.

short: The US Treasury's main bank account at the Federal Reserve, which receives taxes and borrowed money and pays the government's bills.
kid: The town keeps its money in one big jar at the town hall. When the jar fills up, people have a little less in their pockets for a while, and when the town spends from it, the money goes back to them.
detail: The TGA is the federal government's checking account at the Fed. Tax payments and the proceeds of Treasury auctions flow in; spending flows out. Because the account sits outside the banking system, a rising TGA drains bank reserves and money-market liquidity, while a falling TGA adds to them, much like Fed tightening or easing. Markets watch it closely around debt-ceiling episodes. As the limit binds, Treasury runs the balance down, injecting liquidity; once the limit is lifted, Treasury sells a wave of bills to rebuild it, pulling hundreds of billions of dollars out of reserves or the Fed's reverse repo facility, which can strain funding markets and weigh on risky assets. Treasury publishes the balance daily. India's parallel is the Centre's cash balance with the RBI, whose swings around tax dates also move banking liquidity. Common confusion: the TGA is a working cash account, not a savings or wealth fund.
example: Say the TGA has fallen to $300 billion during a debt-ceiling standoff. Once the limit is raised, Treasury aims for $850 billion, so it sells about $550 billion more in bills than it needs for spending. That money comes out of bank reserves or money funds' cash at the Fed, tightening liquidity for a while.

short: When a national government fails to pay interest or principal on its debt on time, or forces lenders to accept worse terms.
kid: Your friend borrowed your toy car and promised to give it back on Friday. Friday comes, and the friend says they can't, or offers back only half the set.
detail: A sovereign default occurs when a government misses a scheduled payment beyond any grace period, or swaps its debt for new bonds worth less, a distressed exchange that rating agencies also treat as default. Unlike a company, a country cannot be liquidated, so default leads to restructuring talks with bondholders, other governments and often the IMF. Examples include Russia's rouble debt default in 1998, Argentina in 2001, Greece's 2012 restructuring, the largest ever, and Sri Lanka in 2022, its first since independence. Foreign-currency debt is the usual problem because a government cannot print dollars; local-currency default is rarer but possible. Consequences include lost market access, a currency slump, stress for banks that hold government bonds, and higher borrowing costs for years. For investors, recovery values and collective action clauses decide losses. Common confusion: a rating downgrade, even to junk, is not a default.
example: Say a country owes bondholders $10 billion and, after missing a payment, offers new bonds with a face value of $7 billion in exchange. That is a 30% haircut on face value: each holder of $1,000 of old bonds gets $700 of new ones.
formula: Haircut on face value = 1 - (Face value of new debt / Face value of old debt)

short: All taxes collected by India's central government in a year, before the states' share is passed on to them.
kid: Before dinner, all the apples from the garden go into one big basket. Then some apples go to the neighbours who helped, and the family keeps what is left.
detail: Gross tax revenue, or GTR, is the total of all taxes the Centre collects: direct taxes such as corporation tax and personal income tax, and indirect taxes such as CGST, customs and excise duties, including cesses and surcharges. It is not what the Centre gets to keep. The states' share of the divisible pool, set by the Finance Commission, is subtracted, along with small transfers to disaster-response funds, to arrive at net tax revenue, the figure that enters the Centre's revenue receipts. Because cesses and surcharges sit outside the divisible pool, the Centre keeps all of them, which is why their rising share annoys states. Markets watch monthly tax data from the Controller General of Accounts to judge whether budget targets will be met. Common confusion: quoting GTR growth as if it were the Centre's own money, when net tax revenue is what funds central spending.
example: Say gross tax revenue is ₹42 lakh crore and the states' share is ₹14 lakh crore, ignoring the small disaster-fund transfers. Net tax revenue to the Centre is ₹28 lakh crore, two-thirds of the gross figure. If gross collections fall short by ₹1.2 lakh crore and states bear a third of the shortfall, the Centre loses ₹0.8 lakh crore of net revenue.
formula: Net tax revenue (to Centre) = Gross tax revenue - States' share of central taxes - Transfers to disaster-response funds

short: Government income that is not from taxes, such as dividends from state-owned firms and the central bank, interest, fees and licence charges.
kid: Most of the class fund comes from everyone chipping in. The rest comes from selling cookies at the school fair and letting other classes borrow its board games.
detail: Non-tax revenue is the part of revenue receipts that does not come from taxation. For India's Centre the largest items are dividends and surplus transfers, especially from the RBI, public sector banks and other state-owned companies; interest on loans to states and public bodies; fees, fines and user charges; and payments for spectrum and other natural resources. Because the RBI transfer can swing by more than ₹1 lakh crore from one year to the next, non-tax revenue is a frequent source of budget surprises, good or bad, and spectrum auction payments can be lumpy too. Investors watch how much the government leans on PSU dividends, since that shapes those companies' payout policies. Common confusion: money from selling shares in PSUs is not non-tax revenue; it is a non-debt capital receipt, because the government gives up an asset rather than earning income from it.
example: Say a government budgets ₹5.5 lakh crore of non-tax revenue: ₹2.6 lakh crore from the RBI, ₹0.7 lakh crore of PSU dividends, ₹0.5 lakh crore of interest and ₹1.7 lakh crore of fees, spectrum and other charges. If the RBI pays ₹0.3 lakh crore more than expected, non-tax revenue rises to ₹5.8 lakh crore.

short: A government's planned year-by-year path for cutting its deficit or debt to a target level, usually set out in its budget.
kid: If you have been eating too many sweets, you don't stop all at once. You plan to eat a few less each day until you are back to just one after dinner.
detail: A glide path turns a fiscal goal into steps, such as cutting the fiscal deficit by half a percentage point of GDP each year; the anchor is the end target it steers toward. Markets and rating agencies judge credibility by whether each step is met. India's FRBM Act set deficit targets that were often relaxed. After the pandemic deficit of 9.2% of GDP in 2020-21, the Centre committed to bring the fiscal deficit below 4.5% by 2025-26, and the 2025-26 budget targeted 4.4%. Under the 2025 plan, from 2026-27 the anchor is debt: central government debt is to fall to about 50% of GDP, plus or minus 1 percentage point, by March 2031. A credible path can lower the risk premium on government bonds and support ratings. Common confusion: a debt anchor allows the deficit to vary from year to year, as long as debt falls along the path.
example: Say a government's deficit is 6% of GDP and it aims for 4.5% in three years. A straight glide path cuts it by 0.5 percentage points a year: to 5.5%, then 5%, then 4.5%. If nominal GDP is ₹300 lakh crore in the final year, the target deficit is ₹13.5 lakh crore.
formula: Annual step = (Starting deficit - Target deficit) / Number of years

short: Goods, services or cash handed out free by governments, often promised before elections, such as free power, loan waivers or monthly cash payments.
kid: Someone running for class monitor promises free sweets for everyone. Free sweets are lovely, but if the class jar pays for them, there may be nothing left for new crayons.
detail: Freebies is the popular Indian term for populist giveaways such as free electricity and water, farm loan waivers, free bus travel for women and monthly cash transfers to women or farmers, especially when announced in election campaigns. The phrase revdi culture entered debate after Prime Minister Narendra Modi used it in 2022, and the Supreme Court has heard petitions on poll-time promises. The fiscal worry is that such schemes are recurring revenue spending, often not fully funded, which crowds out capital spending on roads, schools and hospitals and raises state borrowing; the RBI has flagged the trend in its reports on state finances. Supporters argue that targeted transfers are welfare that lifts consumption and protects the poor. For investors, the trend affects state deficits, SDL supply and rural demand. Common confusion: there is no legal definition, so the line between a freebie and a welfare scheme is political, not technical.
example: Say a state pays ₹1,500 a month to 1 crore women. That costs ₹1,500 crore a month, or ₹18,000 crore a year. If the state's revenue receipts are ₹4 lakh crore, the scheme takes 4.5% of them.

short: A legal limit on government borrowing, best known in Germany's constitution, that caps the yearly deficit except in emergencies.
kid: Your family has a rule: you may only borrow a tiny bit from your sister each week, unless something really bad happens. The rule is stuck on the fridge so nobody forgets.
detail: Germany's debt brake, or Schuldenbremse, was written into the Basic Law in 2009. It limits the federal government's structural deficit, the deficit adjusted for the business cycle, to 0.35% of GDP, and originally barred the states from structural deficits altogether. Extra borrowing is allowed in downturns and, through an escape clause, in emergencies, as in 2020-22. In 2023 the Constitutional Court struck down a plan to shift €60 billion of unused pandemic credit to a climate fund, triggering a budget crisis. In March 2025 parliament loosened the rule: defence spending above 1% of GDP is exempt, a €500 billion infrastructure fund was created, and states may run small deficits. Bund yields jumped on the news. Switzerland has a similar rule. Common confusion: the brake limits new borrowing each year, not the total stock of debt, though over time it pushes debt down.
example: Say German GDP is €4.3 trillion. A 0.35% limit allows a federal structural deficit of about €15 billion. Under the 2025 reform, defence spending above 1% of GDP, or €43 billion, sits outside the limit, so a defence budget of €80 billion would have €37 billion exempt.
formula: Maximum federal structural deficit = 0.35% x Nominal GDP

short: A sweeping US tax-and-spending law, signed in July 2025, that made the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent, trimmed welfare programmes and raised the debt limit.
kid: Sometimes grown-ups put lots of rules into one big book at once: who pays less, who gets less help, and how much the family may borrow. This was one very big book of rules.
detail: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed by President Donald Trump on 4 July 2025, was passed through budget reconciliation, which needs only a simple majority in the Senate. It made permanent the individual income tax cuts of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, added temporary deductions for tips, overtime and car-loan interest, raised the cap on state and local tax deductions, and restored full expensing for equipment and domestic research. It paid for part of this with cuts to Medicaid and food assistance and the phase-out of many clean-energy tax credits from the Inflation Reduction Act, and it raised the debt limit by $5 trillion. The CBO estimated it would add about $3.4 trillion to deficits over 2025-2034, feeding concern about Treasury supply and long-term yields. For India, a 1% tax on cash-funded remittances from 2026 affects some transfers home. Common confusion: many provisions are temporary.
example: The CBO estimated the law would add about $3.4 trillion to federal deficits over 2025-2034, roughly $340 billion a year on average. It also raised the debt limit from about $36.1 trillion to about $41.1 trillion. A migrant sending $1,000 home in cash through a money-transfer shop would pay $10 under the 1% remittance tax.
